title: Ex 8.9 · Intersection distributes over union
prompt: Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be any sets. Prove that $A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$, writing a chain of lines in which each line has exactly the same elements as the one before it.
answer_format: A chain of lines, each a set (like A ∪ (B ∩ C)) or a statement about an element x (like x ∈ A or x ∈ B). Each line must have exactly the same elements as the line before; start from the left side and end at the right side.
hints: Begin with x ∈ A ∩ (B ∪ C): that is, x ∈ A and (x ∈ B or x ∈ C).
Distribute the 'and' over the 'or': P ∧ (Q ∨ R) is the same as (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R).
Each bracket (x ∈ A and x ∈ B) says x ∈ A ∩ B. Finish with the definition of ∪.
solution: Let $x$ be any element. Then $x \in A \cap (B \cup C)$ means $x \in A \land (x \in B \lor x \in C)$.
By the distributive law $P \land (Q \lor R) = (P \land Q) \lor (P \land R)$, this is $(x \in A \land x \in B) \lor (x \in A \land x \in C)$.
That is, $x \in A \cap B$ or $x \in A \cap C$, so $x \in (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$.
Every step was an equivalence, so $A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$. $\blacksquare$

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses Section 8.3 (proving A = B), the definitions of union, intersection and difference (Section 1.5) and the logic laws of Section 2.6.

x ∈ A ∩ B or x ∈ A ∩ C
